text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- About one tenth or 650 jobs will disappear from Arboga, in central western Sweden, after Volvo Aero announced it was moving its Arboga operations to the parent company in Trollhattan. Community leaders estimate about 1,550 people will be forced to leave the town because of Volvo's departure.

- In 1996 unemployment increased in Sweden, according to the labour market committee which has expected a slight fall. The committee said 561,000 people or 13 percent of the workforce were unemployed in 1996 with this number including people on government schemes. In December 1996 the number without regular work was 573,000 which was equivalent to 13.4 percent of the workforce.

- Swedish trade unions defend themselves against criticism after a report by the Organisation of Economic Cooperation and Development said the threat to Sweden's economy was high wage increases and unemployment, but agree rule for the wage negotiations should be looked into.

- A new Hague convention will make it more difficult for estranged parents to kidnap their own children and take them to foreign countries during custody battles. Police recently ordered two Swedish mothers to return their children who they had taken from their American fathers in the U.S..
- The traditional January rally on the bourse gained momentum on Wednesday, with telecommunications firm LM Ericsson's market capitalisation rising 13 billion crowns.

- There is no light on the horizon for Sweden's labour market, with the figure edging up to 13 percent for 1996 from 12.8 in the previous year. The number of unemployed men fell slightly but for woman the number increased.
- The town of Arboga is shocked following Volvo Aero's decision to move its operations to Trollhattan. It will mean a loss of 650 jobs in a region with a population of only 14,300.

- Mining group Trelleborg may seek to spin off its metals and mining group Boliden and list it on the Stockholm bourse, according to newspaper sources. Preparations for the listing are already underway with the move designed to boost Trelleborg's value which has been flat since 1995. These rumours have lifted Trelleborg's share price in recent days.

- Cellular phone user fees will probably fall in Sweden this year, accoridng to Mads Winblad, president of Nokia Mobile phones in Scandinavia. Prices in Norway dipped by 25 percent in Janaury and comments in Denmark indicate lower prices are coming. Winblad said lower prices would make it harder for newcomers in the market.

- Timber group Sodra, Europe's largest pulp exporter, plans to expand its sawmill operation. Over the next three years the company wants to increase its annual production by 150,000 cubic metres to 750,000 cubic metres.
